articles.title: Funding set to double for plan to get rough sleepers off streets by Christmas
articles.summary: Burnham made ending rough sleeping his first pledge when entering Downing Street in July.
articles.content:
Funding is set to double to support a pledge by the prime minister to give every rough sleeper in England a route off the streets by Christmas.

Ending rough sleeping was one of Andy Burnham's first promises when he entered Downing Street, announcing a £442m package to provide emergency accommodation and practical support.

Ahead of the first Rough Sleeping Summit at Downing Street on Monday, No 10 has indicated a further £432m will be added to the initiative in Wednesday's Budget.

Shadow housing secretary Katie Lam said rough sleeping had hit "record highs under Labour" and criticised Burnham for failing to end rough sleeping when he was the Mayor of Greater Manchester.

The most recent official figures estimated there were 4,793 people sleeping rough, external on a single night in autumn 2025 in England.

The government's commitment is that every rough sleeper will either be able to physically move into accommodation by Christmas or will have been offered support as a way to prevent them sleeping rough.

Money being added to the pot this week will extend support beyond March 2027 to the end of this Parliament, taking total investment to £874m.

Burnham told ITV's Good Morning Britain he was confident it could be done, saying: "I have this strong feeling about putting the right standards at the heart of the country again and we can't get to a position where we just become used to walking past people sleeping rough: it's about care for people."

He added: "In the end, actually, it's cheaper to do that than to leave people sleeping rough going in and out of A&E, that's not good for anybody."
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant government commitment to double funding aimed at ending rough sleeping in England by Christmas, which has a broad and meaningful positive impact on vulnerable populations and society. The story focuses on a clear, substantial policy initiative with detailed funding amounts and timelines, addressing a critical social issue with measurable benefits.
articles.personality_title: Government doubles funding to help end rough sleeping in England by Christmas
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Rough sleeping, or sleeping outside without a home, is a serious problem in England. In 2025, nearly 4,800 people were recorded sleeping rough on a single night. The government wants to change this by providing emergency housing and support.

**What happened** – The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, promised to help every rough sleeper find a way off the streets by Christmas. To support this, the government is doubling its funding, adding £432 million to an existing £442 million package. This new money will extend support until 2027, making the total investment £874 million.

**Impact** – This large increase in funding means more people sleeping rough will get a chance to move into safe accommodation or receive support to avoid rough sleeping. It shows a strong commitment to solving a difficult problem and could improve the lives of thousands. Burnham also explained that helping people off the streets can reduce costs for hospitals and emergency services.

**What's next step** – The government will use this money to provide emergency housing and practical help until at least 2027. Officials will also hold meetings, like the Rough Sleeping Summit, to plan and track progress. The goal is that no one will have to sleep rough in England by Christmas.

**One-sentence takeaway** – England is investing nearly £900 million to make sure every person sleeping rough has a safe place or support by Christmas 2025.

articles.title: Climate change rarely goes on trial. This one could be a landmark.
articles.content:
Climate change gets a rare day in court on Monday when 15 Canadian youth will accuse the federal government of violating their constitutional rights by failing to adequately address the country’s role in global warming. Although thousands of similar cases have been filed across the globe, legal experts said this long-awaited case is arguably the most consequential to reach trial.

The lawsuit is the latest in a yearslong campaign by young people who are using the courts to force elected officials to mitigate climate change. Like similar cases in the United States, including the landmark Held v. Montana, the plaintiffs in La Rose v. His Majesty the King argue that the government has violated their constitutional rights by allowing the crisis to continue.

Set in Vancouver, the proceedings are slated to last five weeks, with the 15 plaintiffs expected to testify alongside climate scientists and other experts. “It’s the chance for the young people to tell their story,” said Kelly Matheson, deputy director for global strategy at Our Children’s Trust, the nonprofit behind this case and many similar efforts around the world.

The outcome, while not precedent setting outside of Canada, could prove persuasive in other climate litigation or spur new cases. “We found that some of the positive decisions from some countries have been inspirational in other countries,” said Michael Gerrard, faculty director of the Columbia University’s Sabin Center for Climate Change Law. “This trial will be closely watched.”

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

The case began in 2019, when the youth, six of whom identify as Indigenous, filed suit. They alleged, among other things, that by not doing enough to combat climate change, the government had violated Section 7 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, which guarantees “the right to life, liberty, and security of the person”. They also argued that federal action breached their equality protections granted under Section 15 of the charter because, as young people, they will bear a disproportionate share of the impacts of the crisis.

The original lawsuit took aim at much of Canada’s approach to climate change. The plaintiffs argued that the government had allowed emissions to remain dangerously high, set targets that fell short of what scientists said was necessary to avoid the worst outcomes, repeatedly failed to meet those targets, and continued supporting the development and expansion of fossil fuels.

Although the government did not challenge the reality of climate change, its arguments included a claim that the accusations were overly broad and the lawsuit improperly asked the court to resolve a political matter. A federal judge agreed and dismissed the case without a trial in 2020. The plaintiffs appealed. In 2023, the Federal Court of Appeal upheld the dismissal of the Section 15 claim but allowed the Section 7 arguments to proceed if the plaintiffs more specifically detailed the government conduct that violated their protected rights.

The plaintiffs amended their complaint to focus on the Canadian Net-Zero Emissions Accountability Act of 2021, which commits the country to achieving the law’s objectives by 2050, and the 2030 emissions reduction plan adopted under that law. They argue that the efforts don’t go far enough to avoid violating their Charter rights in the context of climate change and that the government committed to in the Act.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

“Increasingly, people across Canada and the world are seeing the direct impacts of climate change,” said Andrew Gage, a staff lawyer for West Coast Environment Law who has worked on this case alongside Our Children’s Trust. “The plaintiffs will have their day in court.”

The Canadian Department of Justice referred a request for comment to Environment and Climate Change Canada, which declined an interview request but provided a written statement to Grist. “Our commitment to net-zero by 2050 has not wavered, and we are implementing an ambitious climate agenda,” its spokesperson, Samantha Bayard, wrote in an email. “The Government of Canada respects the role of the courts, the right of Canadians to bring matters before the courts, and the important role that an independent judiciary plays in our democracy.”

All 15 youths, who were between the ages of 10 and 19 when the suit was filed, are expected to testify. They will be joined by expert witnesses in climate science, renewable energy, children’s health, and economics. Closing arguments are scheduled for February with a decision expected sometime in 2027, although an appeal could delay a resolution. Still, it is unusual for such a case to even be heard.

“Seldom has climate been put on trial,” said James May, an environmental law professor at Washburn University who isn’t involved in this case but has supported some of Our Children’s Trust’s past work. He estimated that more than 3,000 climate cases have been filed worldwide over the past few decades, but most never reached a courtroom. The Hawai’i state Department of Transportation, for example, settled a lawsuit filed by 13 young people and agreed to develop a plan to zero out emissions from the transportation sector by 2045. The landmark Juliana v. the United States was dismissed after years of litigation and the Supreme Court declined to consider it.

Held v. Montana was a rare exception. After a seven-day trial in 2023, a judge ruled that the state’s energy permitting policies violated the plaintiffs’ right to “a clean and healthful environment,” which is enshrined in the state constitution. The state supreme court upheld that decision in 2024.

A similar outcome in Vancouver could have implications in other British commonwealth countries and beyond, said Matheson. “These courts are looking to each other,” she said. “There is momentum building.”

But even if the plaintiffs don’t win, May considers the trial a victory even before it starts. “It could serve as a blueprint for how to do this elsewhere,” he said. “It has already succeeded.”

articles.personality_title: Canadian youth take government to court over climate change
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Fifteen young people in Canada are suing the federal government because they believe it is not doing enough to fight climate change. They say this failure harms their rights under Canada’s constitution.

**What happened** – The case, called La Rose v. His Majesty the King, began in 2019 and went to trial in Vancouver in early 2024. The youths, aged 10 to 19 when they filed the lawsuit, argue the government broke laws that protect their right to life and equality by allowing pollution to stay high and not meeting climate goals. The trial will last about five weeks, with the youths and experts speaking.

**Impact** – This case is rare because most climate lawsuits never get to court. It is important because it challenges the government’s climate actions using legal rights, not just politics. If successful, it could influence other countries with similar legal systems and encourage more young people to demand stronger climate actions.

**What’s next step** – After the trial ends in February, a decision is expected by 2027, though appeals could delay it. Regardless of the outcome, the case is already serving as an example for future climate lawsuits worldwide.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Canadian youth are using the courts to hold their government accountable for climate change, potentially setting a new example for climate justice cases globally.

Ces jeunes, âgés de 10 à 19 ans lors du dépôt de la plainte, soutiennent que le gouvernement a violé leurs droits à la vie et à l’égalité en maintenant des niveaux élevés de pollution et en ne respectant pas ses objectifs climatiques. articles.title: NYC food pantries are now stocking pet food for struggling households
articles.summary:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM If you’ve ever moved a bit of food off your own plate just so your dog could eat, too, then you know the feeling this program is trying to address. It’s a pretty common one in New York City right now. And most people who surrender a pet to […]
The post NYC food pantries are now stocking pet food for struggling households first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

If you’ve ever moved a bit of food off your own plate just so your dog could eat, too, then you know the feeling this program is trying to address. It’s a pretty common one in New York City right now. And most people who surrender a pet to a shelter aren’t doing it lightly. They do it as the very last resort, when they’ve truly run out of ways to make it work.

NYC has put $500,000 toward the problem. The city is funding 22 food pantries across all five boroughs to stock and distribute free pet food, with supplies expected to start arriving within about two weeks.

Teddy and everyone like him

Cassandra, a Brooklyn resident, has a three-year-old Shih Tzu named Teddy, who she’s had since he was two months old. “Sometimes I have to sacrifice a little of my food that way he doesn’t go hungry, until I can get more food for him,” she said. At The Campaign Against Hunger in Brooklyn, pantry director Tamara Dawson has watched the same dynamic for years. “They bring their pets with them and are feeding them online because they have been without,” she said.

The organization already offers free pet food to clients, but the supply has always depended on chasing grants and donors. The city funding makes that a little less precarious.

What happened after SNAP cuts

St. John’s Bread and Life in Brooklyn received a $17,000 voucher through the initiative. Staff said demand has grown since many clients saw their SNAP benefits reduced, something that moved through the whole household budget, pets included.

“The affordability crisis affects every member of a family, including the pets we love,” said Mayor Zohran Mamdani. “No New Yorker should have to choose between feeding themselves and feeding their pets.”

Animal welfare groups have tracked the connection between financial hardship and shelter surrender for years. Getting pet food to families early is a pretty practical way to keep that from happening.

Where to find free pet food in NYC

Here are all 22 participating locations:

Bronx

– Part of the Solution: 2759 Webster Ave., 10458

– New York Common Pantry: 1290 Hoe Ave., 10459

– Davidson Community Center: 2038 Davidson Ave., 10453

– The Kingsbridge Heights Community Center: 3067 Kingsbridge Terrace, 10463

Queens

– River Fund: 89-11 Lefferts Boulevard, 11418

– Yeshua Worldwide Ministries Food Pantry: 7911 Caldwell Ave., 11379

– Hour Children Community Outreach: 36-49 11th Street, 11106

Brooklyn

– Community Help in Park Slope: 200 Fourth Ave., 11217

– Metropolitan Council on Jewish Poverty: 5361 Preston Court, 11234

– On the Go Relief: 2832 Fulton Street, 11207

– St. John’s Bread and Life Food Pantry: 795 Lexington Ave., 11221

– The Campaign Against Hunger: 2004 Fulton Street, 11233

– YMCA Community Market: 2980 West 29th Street, 11224

Manhattan

– Holy Apostles Soup Kitchen Pantry: 296 Ninth Ave., 10001

– New York Common Pantry: 8 East 109th Street, 10029

– St. Clemens Food Pantry: 423 West 46th Street, 10036

– The Father’s Heart Ministries: 543-545 East 11th Street, 10009

– The Lower Eastside Girls Club: 402 East 8th Street, 10009

– Trinity’s Services and Food for the Homeless: 602 East 9th Street, 10009

Staten Island

– Project Hospitality: 205 Canal Street, 10304

– Feeding with TLC: 309 St. Paul’s Ave., 10304

Call ahead if you’re not sure what to bring or whether your nearest location is stocked yet. And if someone you know could use this, it’s the kind of thing that’s good to pass along.

articles.title: Vote young yet govern much later: West African youth’s struggle for power
articles.summary: Young people are deemed mature enough to elect their leaders, yet not to replace them. They drive political movements forward by voting, advocating, campaigning, and protesting, yet cannot run for office themselves.
articles.content:
In West Africa, young people can vote for the first time at 18. In some states, they are eligible to serve in parliament by age 25. However, depending on the country, they must wait until they are 35, 40, or even 50 years old before being eligible to run for the highest office. Although these age limits are beginning to shift, the real challenges often lie deeper in the electoral structure.

Young people are deemed mature enough to elect their leaders, yet not to replace them. They drive political movements forward by voting, advocating, campaigning, and protesting, yet cannot run for office themselves. The question is, can democracy really be called inclusive when it gives young people the right to elect but not to be elected?

Age: A shifting barrier

Across the region, the voting age is 18. However, presidential eligibility ages vary widely. In Gambia, it’s 30; in Senegal, Nigeria, and Côte d’Ivoire, it’s 35; and in Benin, Ghana, and Guinea, it’s 40. In the legislative assemblies, the bar is even lower. In Togo, Benin, Senegal, and Nigeria’s House of Representatives, it’s 25, while in Ghana it’s 21.

The situation in Togo requires closer inspection. On May 6, 2024, the country legally became a parliamentary republic. Under the 2024 Constitution, the eligibility age for President of the Republic is 50. Parliament also now elects the president, whose powers are limited. Authority now rests with the President of the Council of Ministers, who must be at least 40 and is not elected in public presidential elections. Faure Gnassingbé has held this position since May 3, 2025, the day parliament also elected the country’s oldest-ever incoming president of the Republic, Jean-Lucien Savi de Tové, 86.

However, the country’s legal age limit is hardly set in stone. In 2002, the National Assembly lowered it from 45 to 35 — a reform the opposition called tailor-made for Faure Gnassingbé.

More recently, in Ghana’s capital, Accra, on July 30, 2026, the Ghanaian government agreed in principle to lower the minimum presidential eligibility age from 40 to 35, defying the Constitutional Review Committee’s recommendation of 30. This legislation will ultimately go to a referendum, requiring a 40 percent turnout and a 75 percent approval.

In 2018, Nigeria set a regional precedent. Under pressure from the youth-led Not Too Young To Run campaign, the law lowered the presidential eligibility age from 40 to 35 and the House of Representatives’ eligibility age from 30 to 25.

According to data from the Inter-Parliamentary Union, lowering the minimum presidential age leads to younger parliaments. However, Côte d’Ivoire tells a very different story. In 2016, after removing the maximum age limit of 75 to run for office, incumbent President Alassane Ouattara, 83, ran for another term in 2025. The law rarely protects younger generations.

Youths particularly active in street movements

Even though young people have the right to vote across the continent, that does not mean all young people exercise that right. In August 2025, an Afrobarometer survey found that those aged 18 to 35 were less active than their elders in almost all traditional means of political participation. Overall across the continent, they trailed by 18 percentage points in voting, but by a record 29 points in Senegal. Protests were the only exception.

In Togo’s capital of Lomé, the June 6 Movement, sparked by the rapper Aamron’s arrest, brought thousands of people onto the streets. According to the Media Foundation for West Africa, the subsequent crackdown, for which the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) blamed government-backed militiamen, left seven dead.

Similarly, in Madagascar, the September 2025 protests toppled President Andry Rajoelina’s government, resulting in a military takeover. According to the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), the overthrown president himself came to power in 2019 on the back of a protest, at just 34 years old.

Comparably, in Kenya, street protests forced the withdrawal of the 2024 Finance Bill. Meanwhile, in Morocco, youth-led protests prompted the authorities to announce youth candidacy incentives and prosecute specific ringleaders.

Although leaderless movements wrest concessions, they rarely last without political parties or trade unions to sustain them.

The gap between participation and representation

The Inter-Parliamentary Report, published on April 9, 2026, found that elected officials aged 30 and under account for just 2.8 percent of all parliamentarians worldwide. Since 2023, progress has stalled for the first time since 2014. More than a third (37.1 percent) of legislative houses have no parliamentarians in this age group.

The lack of youth representation and participation is a significant challenge considering young people under 35 account for roughly 70 percent of West Africa’s population, according to the West Africa Youth Democracy Conference.

According to data from the Inter-Parliamentary Union (IPU), at the start of Ghana’s 2025 parliamentary term, despite the legal minimum age of 21, no parliamentarians were aged 30 or under. What’s more, those aged 31 to 40 held just 46 of the 269 parliamentary seats, or 17.1 percent. After Senegal’s 2024 legislative elections, the National Assembly had only five members under 30, accounting for just 3 percent. Although almost 38 percent of registered voters were aged 18 to 35, the Assembly’s average age was 47. Elected at just 44, the country’s youngest-ever president, Bassirou Diomaye Faye, only became an official candidate after his mentor, Ousmane Sonko, was disqualified.

In Nigeria, International IDEA, an intergovernmental organization that supports sustainable democracy worldwide, reported that in 2015, only three of the 360 members of the House of Representatives were between the ages of 18–25, rising to 14 in 2019 — a positive but modest development.

In Dakar, the head of Yiaga Africa, the organization behind the Not Too Young to Run campaign, summed up the situation, stating that the political arena is more open on paper than in reality.

However, Afrobarometer has identified a paradox. While young people do vote less than their elders, they are also excluded from seats of power and the polls. This representation gap is anything but passive; it breeds disengagement. The IPU warns that young people’s absence from parliamentary assemblies undermines institutional legitimacy and jeopardizes trust in democracy. Senegal, listed in the 2026 IPU report as one of the countries where parliament grew younger in the most recent elections, shows that rejuvenation is possible when a political agenda empowers a generation.

Rewriting the deal: money, parties, obstacles

High age limit proponents demand experience. Across the 34 countries that Afrobarometer surveyed, citizens favor an average leadership age of 39. Those calling for a lower age limit seek proven engagement measures, such as lowering the eligibility age, quotas, and forums for young parliamentarians. However, as Nigeria shows, often, the main obstacle is financial.

Nigeria’s ruling party, the All Progressives Congress (APC), has set the total cost of its 2027 presidential nomination and expression-of-interest forms at NGN 100 million (USD 75,000), NGN 30 million (USD 22,521) for the expression of interest, and NGN 70 million (USD 52,550) for the nomination. The Senate will cost NGN 20 million (USD 15,014) and the House of Representatives NGN 10 million (USD 7,507).

Young people will receive a 50 percent discount only on nomination fees, leaving the presidential bill at NGN 65 million (USD 48,789). A Nigerian civil society group calculated that workers earning the minimum wage, NGN 70,000 (USD 52) per month, would have to work for more than a century to buy some of these forms.

The Electoral Act, 2026, signed on February 18, also doubled the presidential candidate’s campaign spending limit to NGN 10 billion (USD 7.5 million) and tripled that of governorship candidates to NGN 3 billion (USD 2.2 million).

At the initiative of ECOWAS and the youth-led advocacy organization Legis360, delegates from 12 countries gathered in Dakar to bring these obstacles to the forefront. In their communiqué, they launched the West Africa Youth Observer Network (WAYON) and called for youth quotas, reduced candidate fees, and spending limits. ECOWAS later announced it would deploy youth-only election observers for Nigeria’s upcoming presidential election on January 16, 2027.

Other countries exemplify how laws can directly impact nominations. According to the IPU, Ecuador owes much of its progress to a 2022 law, which required 25 percent of its candidates to be young adults. Countries with term limits also have considerably more young parliamentarians than the global average. In 2023, the IPU also noted that limited youth funding and a lack of spending limits contributed to aging parliamentary assemblies.

Elsewhere, the obstacles are political. Take, for example, Benin. After disqualifying the main opposition candidate (Les Démocrates) for failing to meet election requirements, current President Romuald Wadagni faced only one opponent (Paul Hounkpe). On April 12, 2026, Wadagni subsequently won the presidential election with 94.27 percent of the vote. In 2024, a constitutional reform that extended the presidential term from five to seven years also raised the minimum vote threshold for securing seats in the National Assembly from 10 percent of parliamentary election votes to 20 percent. This regulation far outweighs a candidate’s date of birth when they have no party machine behind them.

Another example is Burkina Faso. In January 2026, the military junta dissolved all political parties. Meanwhile, in The Gambia, President Barrow will run for a third term in the December 5 presidential election.

Inclusive voting, but flawed representation

Is a system that gives young people the right to elect their leader but impedes their ability to become one themselves fully inclusive? The findings speak for themselves. Although Nigeria has lowered its age limits and Ghana has committed to doing the same, these limits are more a symptom than a cause. Age is not the sole contributing factor.

Critics argue that lowering age limits without also addressing nomination costs, party regulations, and the openness of the political arena would only be the first step on a seemingly endless staircase. What stands between young people and decision-making positions are exceedingly high costs, restrictive nomination practices, candidate exclusions, and even the lack of parties.

Until street movements have credible institutional representatives, they will continue to wrest temporary concessions or, as seen in Madagascar, give way to powers other than those they had hoped for. The primary challenge of the West African Democratic Pact is making young people not only the promised future of politics, but also an active part of today’s representation.

The detailed context and examples provide substance and illustrate both challenges and hopeful developments.
articles.personality_title: West African youth push for fairer access to political power
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – In West Africa, young people can vote from age 18 but often must wait much longer to run for important government positions. This creates a gap between their power as voters and their chances to become leaders.

**What happened** – Countries in West Africa have different age rules for running for president or parliament. For example, Nigeria lowered the presidential minimum age from 40 to 35 after youth campaigns. Ghana plans to lower its age limit too. Despite these changes, many young people still face high costs and political barriers that make it hard to run for office.

**Impact** – Young people make up about 70% of West Africa’s population but hold very few government seats. This lack of representation can make young voters feel disconnected from politics. However, youth-led movements and new laws show progress. For instance, protests in some countries have influenced political change, and regional groups are calling for fairer rules and lower fees to help young candidates.

**What's next step** – Efforts continue to lower age limits and reduce financial and political obstacles for young candidates. Organizations like ECOWAS and youth groups are working together to improve youth participation. Upcoming elections, such as Nigeria’s in 2027, will test these changes and may encourage more young leaders to emerge.

**One-sentence takeaway** – While West African youth face challenges in becoming elected leaders, ongoing reforms and youth activism are opening doors for greater political inclusion.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les jeunes d’Afrique de l’Ouest revendiquent un accès plus juste au pouvoir politique
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – En Afrique de l’Ouest, les jeunes peuvent voter dès 18 ans, mais doivent souvent attendre beaucoup plus longtemps pour se présenter à des postes importants. Cela crée un écart entre leur pouvoir de voter et leurs chances de devenir dirigeants.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Les pays d’Afrique de l’Ouest ont des règles d’âge différentes pour être président ou député. Par exemple, le Nigeria a abaissé l’âge minimum présidentiel de 40 à 35 ans après des campagnes de jeunes. Le Ghana prévoit aussi de baisser cette limite. Malgré ces changements, beaucoup de jeunes font face à des coûts élevés et des barrières politiques qui compliquent leur candidature.

**Impact** – Les jeunes représentent environ 70 % de la population ouest-africaine, mais occupent très peu de sièges gouvernementaux. Ce manque de représentation peut les éloigner de la politique. Pourtant, les mouvements de jeunesse et les nouvelles lois montrent des progrès. Par exemple, des manifestations ont influencé des changements politiques, et des groupes régionaux demandent des règles plus justes et des frais réduits pour aider les jeunes candidats.

**Prochaine étape** – Les efforts se poursuivent pour abaisser les limites d’âge et réduire les obstacles financiers et politiques pour les jeunes candidats. Des organisations comme la CEDEAO et des groupes de jeunesse collaborent pour améliorer la participation des jeunes. Les prochaines élections, comme celle du Nigeria en 2027, testeront ces changements et pourraient encourager plus de jeunes leaders.

**En une phrase** – Bien que les jeunes d’Afrique de l’Ouest rencontrent des difficultés pour devenir élus, les réformes en cours et l’activisme des jeunes ouvrent la voie à une plus grande inclusion politique.
articles.personality_title_es: Los jóvenes de África Occidental luchan por un acceso más justo al poder político
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – En África Occidental, los jóvenes pueden votar a los 18 años, pero a menudo deben esperar mucho más tiempo para postularse a cargos importantes. Esto crea una brecha entre su poder como votantes y sus oportunidades para convertirse en líderes.

**Qué pasó** – Los países de África Occidental tienen diferentes edades mínimas para postularse a la presidencia o al parlamento. Por ejemplo, Nigeria bajó la edad presidencial de 40 a 35 años tras campañas juveniles. Ghana también planea reducir este límite. A pesar de estos cambios, muchos jóvenes enfrentan altos costos y barreras políticas que dificultan postularse.

**Impacto** – Los jóvenes constituyen alrededor del 70 % de la población de África Occidental, pero ocupan muy pocos cargos en el gobierno. Esta falta de representación puede hacer que los jóvenes se sientan alejados de la política. Sin embargo, los movimientos juveniles y nuevas leyes muestran avances. Por ejemplo, protestas en algunos países han influido en cambios políticos, y grupos regionales piden reglas más justas y tarifas más bajas para ayudar a los jóvenes candidatos.

**Próximo paso** – Continúan los esfuerzos para bajar los límites de edad y reducir los obstáculos financieros y políticos para los jóvenes candidatos. Organizaciones como ECOWAS y grupos juveniles trabajan juntos para mejorar la participación juvenil. Las próximas elecciones, como las de Nigeria en 2027, pondrán a prueba estos cambios y podrían fomentar más líderes jóvenes.

**Una frase clave** – Aunque los jóvenes de África Occidental enfrentan desafíos para ser elegidos, las reformas en marcha y el activismo juvenil están abriendo puertas para una mayor inclusión política.
